open_obligations: Note that Liang et al.'s judge-managed two-debater MAD differs from N-agent voting.
Check the independence assumption against real LLM samples.
Check whether more agents help when the correct answer is not the modal one.
in.other_title: Majority voting success probability approaches 1 as the number of agents grows
in.rationale: Liang et al. list scheduling more agents as future work. Choi, Zhu and Li prove that majority voting over N homogeneous independent agents picks the correct answer with probability at least 1 - exp(-N (Delta/sqrt(K) - 1/sqrt(N))^2) when N > K/Delta^2, and find debate adds little beyond voting; Liang et al.'s MAD has two adversarial debaters and a judge, not N voters.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: how adding more agents affects multi-agent decisions, for majority voting over independent LLM agents

open_obligations: Note that alignment is measured as classification PGR, not value alignment.
Check whether debate here is adversarial with assigned sides, unlike Liang et al.'s tit-for-tat MAD.
Check the cost of two debater instances, which Lang et al. flag.
in.other_title: Debate transcripts from a strong model help train a better weak supervisor
in.rationale: Liang et al. list using debate as AI feedback for alignment as future work. Lang, Huang and Li use debate transcripts from Qwen-14B as context to train a better Qwen-7B weak supervisor whose labels then train the strong model, reporting better alignment on OpenAI weak-to-strong benchmarks; the 'alignment' target is binary classification accuracy, not preference alignment.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate can serve as AI feedback for model alignment, for weak-to-strong training on NLP classification
